title: Sealing Exposed Aggregate Driveways and Patios
metaTitle: Sealing Exposed Aggregate Driveways and Patios
metaDescription: How sealing protects exposed aggregate driveways and patios in Southwestern Ontario, including finish choice, the process, and how often to reseal.
excerpt: Exposed aggregate has more surface texture than any other concrete finish, which changes how it should be sealed. Here is what makes this surface different and how to keep it protected.
heroAlt: Sealed exposed aggregate driveway with stones enhanced and water beading on the surface
keyTakeaways: Exposed aggregate has the deepest surface texture of any common decorative concrete finish, which means it holds more dirt, moisture and road salt if left unsealed.
A solvent-based acrylic sealer penetrates into the gaps around each exposed stone rather than sitting only on the surface, which matters more on aggregate than on smoother finishes.
Sealing enhances the natural colour variation in the stones themselves, not just the surrounding concrete paste, which is part of why exposed aggregate looks noticeably richer once sealed.
Because of the exposed texture, exposed aggregate driveways often need resealing toward the more frequent end of the typical 2- to 4-year cycle, especially where road salt is used through winter.

A non-slip additive is worth considering on exposed aggregate patios and walkways even though the texture already provides some grip, since a glossy sealer film can still create a slick surface when wet.

body.text: Exposed aggregate is a popular choice for driveways and patios across Southwestern Ontario because of the natural stone texture it brings to a concrete surface. Instead of a smooth or stamped finish, exposed aggregate reveals the actual stones embedded in the concrete mix, creating a surface with real depth and visual interest that most other finishes cannot match. That same texture, though, makes exposed aggregate one of the more demanding surfaces to seal properly. The gaps and irregularities between stones give dirt, moisture and de-icing salt more places to collect than a flat surface would, which makes a properly applied, breathable sealer more important here than on almost any other concrete finish.
What makes exposed aggregate different to seal

Every exposed stone in an aggregate surface creates a small edge and a slight depression around it where the surrounding concrete paste was washed or brushed away during installation. Multiplied across an entire driveway or patio, that adds up to significantly more surface area and texture than a smooth or lightly broomed finish. Sealer needs to get into those gaps, not just coat the tops of the stones, or the surface ends up with uneven protection, more visible than an inconsistent seal job on a flatter surface would be. This is one of the clearest places where the type of sealer matters. A solvent-based acrylic sealer penetrates more deeply than a water-based product, which allows it to work into the texture around each stone rather than bridging over the top and missing the low points.
How sealing enhances exposed aggregate specifically

On a plain concrete surface, sealer mostly enhances the colour of the concrete paste itself. On exposed aggregate, sealer also enhances the natural colour and variation of the stones, which is often the whole reason a homeowner chose this finish in the first place. Wetting the stones with sealer brings out colour tones, from warm browns and greys to occasional flecks of other minerals, that are much less visible on dry, unsealed aggregate. This effect is strongest with a gloss finish, which produces the deepest colour saturation and the most pronounced wet-look appearance, though semi-gloss also enhances stone colour with a more moderate satin sheen. A matte finish will still protect the surface and add some richness to the stones without the higher shine. All three finishes are detailed further at /finishes, and the choice often comes down to how much shine a homeowner wants on a driveway that is visible from the street every day.
The sealing process on an aggregate surface

Preparation matters more on exposed aggregate than on smoother surfaces because of how easily dirt and organic growth can lodge in the texture. Pressure washing needs to be thorough enough to clear debris out of the gaps between stones, not just clean the surface film off the top. The surface is then given time to dry fully, which can take longer on aggregate than on flat concrete since moisture can sit in the low points around each stone longer than it would on an open, flat surface. Any repairs are addressed and surrounding areas masked before sealer is applied with a sprayer and back-rolled by hand. The back-rolling step is particularly important on aggregate, since it works sealer down into the texture around each stone and avoids the pooling or uneven coverage that spray-only application can leave on an irregular surface. Once applied, the surface is dry to the touch within 1 to 2 hours, ready for foot traffic the next day, and can handle vehicles after 48 to 72 hours. Application happens when the surface is dry and temperatures are roughly 10 to 30 degrees Celsius, which typically means spring or fall in this region.

Because exposed aggregate holds more debris and moisture in its texture than smoother finishes, a thorough pressure wash and full drying time before sealing matter even more here than on a stamped or broom-finished surface.
How often exposed aggregate needs resealing

Most concrete surfaces in this region fall into a 2- to 4-year reseal cycle, and exposed aggregate tends to sit toward the more frequent end of that range, particularly on driveways. The texture that makes aggregate attractive also means road salt, tire wear and freeze-thaw cycling have more surface area to act on than they would on a smooth driveway. Signs it is time to reseal include water no longer beading on the surface, a general dulling of the stone colour that used to look vibrant, and a rougher, more porous feel underfoot in the gaps between stones. Because the solvent-based sealer re-emulsifies previous solvent-based coats, a properly timed recoat bonds seamlessly into the existing layer, which keeps the texture and colour consistent rather than building up an uneven film over multiple applications.
Exposed aggregate driveways and winter salt

Southwestern Ontario winters mean road salt is a fact of life for most driveways, and exposed aggregate's texture gives salt more places to sit against the concrete than a smooth surface would. A properly sealed aggregate driveway resists salt penetration far better than an unsealed one, since the sealer forms a barrier between the salt and the concrete and stone beneath it. This matters most in the months right after a fresh application, which is part of why timing a reseal before winter, in the fall application window while temperatures still sit above 10 degrees Celsius, tends to give the best protection through the season that follows. More on how sealing addresses salt and freeze-thaw specifically is covered in our related guide on road salt and freeze-thaw protection.
Grip and non-slip considerations

Exposed aggregate naturally has more texture and grip than a smooth or lightly broomed surface, which is one of its practical advantages on a driveway or walkway. That said, a glossy sealer film applied over aggregate can still reduce grip when the surface is wet, since the sealer smooths over some of the microtexture between the stones even as the stones themselves remain textured. A non-slip additive can be blended into any finish for anyone concerned about slip resistance, particularly on aggregate patios near pools or walkways that see winter foot traffic. Our companion guide on non-slip additives goes into more detail on how that works.
Exposed aggregate patios versus driveways

An exposed aggregate patio and an exposed aggregate driveway share the same core sealing needs but face different demands. A patio mostly deals with foot traffic, UV exposure and weather, which generally means it holds its seal a bit longer than a driveway does. A driveway adds tire wear, vehicle weight and, critically, winter road salt to that list, which is why driveways in this material tend to need attention more often. Both benefit from the same solvent-based acrylic sealer and back-roll application method, and TriCity handles both regularly across the region, from patios in Stratford and Ingersoll to driveways in Tillsonburg and St. Marys. More detail on driveway sealing specifically is available at /services/exposed-aggregate-sealing, and patio-specific information is at /services/patio-sealing.
New aggregate versus older, weathered surfaces

A newly poured exposed aggregate driveway or patio and an older one that has gone several years without sealing require slightly different approaches. On new concrete, sealing typically happens once the concrete has cured sufficiently, and the first application tends to produce a dramatic improvement since the stones have not yet been dulled by weather or traffic. On an older, weathered surface, the pressure washing step becomes more important, since years of accumulated dirt, algae or mineral staining in the texture need to be cleared before sealer can properly penetrate and bond. In some cases a weathered aggregate surface benefits from a more thorough cleaning process before the standard sealing steps begin, which a site assessment can identify ahead of time.
Protecting an exposed aggregate investment

Exposed aggregate is a premium finish, and keeping it properly sealed is what preserves both its appearance and its resistance to the wear this region's climate creates. faq.q: Why does exposed aggregate need more frequent sealing than other concrete finishes?
faq.a: The texture around each exposed stone gives dirt, moisture and road salt more surface area to act on than a smooth or lightly textured finish. Driveways in particular, which also face tire wear and winter salt, often need resealing toward the more frequent end of the typical 2- to 4-year cycle.

faq.q: Does sealing change the colour of the stones in exposed aggregate?
faq.a: Yes. Sealer enhances the natural colour and variation in the stones themselves, not just the surrounding concrete paste. A gloss finish produces the most pronounced colour saturation, semi-gloss gives a more moderate satin enhancement, and matte protects the surface with minimal added sheen.

faq.q: Is exposed aggregate slippery when sealed?
faq.a: The stone texture provides natural grip, but a glossy sealer film can still reduce traction when wet. A non-slip additive can be blended into any of the three finishes for extra slip resistance on patios, walkways or pool surrounds.

faq.q: How long should I wait before driving on a newly sealed exposed aggregate driveway?
faq.a: The surface is dry to the touch within 1 to 2 hours and safe for foot traffic the next day, but vehicles should stay off for 48 to 72 hours to let the sealer fully cure.

faq.q: Can old, faded exposed aggregate be restored with sealing?
faq.a: In most cases, yes. A thorough pressure wash followed by a fresh coat of solvent-based acrylic sealer typically restores much of the original colour depth in both the stones and the surrounding concrete, provided the surface itself is still structurally sound.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to seal an exposed aggregate driveway in this region?
faq.a: Sealing should happen when the surface is dry and temperatures are roughly 10 to 30 degrees Celsius, which in Southwestern Ontario typically means spring or fall. Sealing before winter is especially useful for driveways facing road salt exposure.
